title: Pauri 1, sound: anand bhaiaa
hook: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand, the song of bliss, and your line, bliss, together. Today, the very first line, just its sound.

A song can get into a person long before they understand a word of it. A lullaby in a language you don't speak. A chant at a stadium. The first bars of a tune your grandmother hummed in the kitchen. The sound arrives first, and the meaning catches up later, sometimes years later. Plenty of Sikh kids can sing the opening of Anand Sahib long before anyone explains it to them. So today, before a single word of meaning, just the sound.
screen: `A SONG GETS IN BEFORE THE WORDS.` → `SOUND FIRST, MEANING LATER.` → `TODAY, JUST THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, transliterated: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa. Walk through its sounds. Anand, stress on the second syllable: a-NUND. Bhaiaa: bha-I-aa, three soft beats; it means has happened, has come. Meree maae: MAY-ree MAA-ay, my mother, a call, the way you'd call to someone in the next room. Then satguroo: sat-GU-roo, the True Guru. Mai: me, I. Paaiaa: PAA-i-aa, have found. Hear the music in it. Bhaiaa in the middle, paaiaa at the end: the line rhymes with itself, and the long aa sounds keep opening, like a mouth that's singing rather than speaking. It's written in a raag, Ramkali, to be sung. Its last line comes back almost to the start: kahai Naanak anand hoaa, satguroo mai paaiaa. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. The circle closes on the sound it opened with, and every pauri of Anand Sahib ends with kahai Naanak, says Nanak. One more detail. Guru Amar Das wrote this, not Guru Nanak. But in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Gurus who wrote after Guru Nanak sign their verses with his name. The Granth marks the writer with a number, Mahala three for Guru Amar Das, but the name in the verse is always Nanak. Sikhs understand that as one light passing from Guru to Guru: words of the third Guru, signed with the name of the first.
screen: `A-NUND BHA-I-AA MAY-REE MAA-AY.` · `BHAIAA AND PAAIAA: IT RHYMES.` · `EVERY PAURI ENDS: KAHAI NAANAK.` · `THE THIRD GURU SIGNS AS NANAK.` · then, large: `ANAND BHAIAA.`

segments.voice: Breathe in, and on the out-breath say it slowly: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa, letting the long aa sounds open; it doesn't need to be perfect. Say it once more, and if you like, let it tip into a tune, or just repeat the first two words, anand bhaiaa, softly. If you pray, follow it with Waheguru, then sit in the quiet after the sound.
Satguroo, the True Guru. The opening of Anand Sahib, learned by sound: anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa, with every pauri ending kahai Naanak.
Your line: anand bhaiaa. Joy has come, in a sound small enough to hum. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs learn the opening of Anand Sahib by ear in childhood, singing it at the close of services; in kirtan it is sung in Raag Ramkali or in simpler congregational tunes.
